section.heading: 3.2. The Product and Quotient Rules
section.paragraph: In this section, we study two more rules of differentiation: the Product Rule and the Quotient Rule.
section.heading: The Product Rule
section.paragraph: The derivative of the product of two differentiable functions is given by the following rule:
The derivative of the product of two functions is the first function times the derivative of the second plus the second function times the derivative of the first.
The Product Rule may be extended to the case involving the product of any finite number of functions (see Exercise 73). We prove the Product Rule at the end of this section.
The derivative of the product of two functions is not given by the product of the derivatives of the functions; that is, in general
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack \neq f^{\prime}(x)g^{\prime}(x)$$
For example, if $$f(x) = x$$ and $$g(x) = 2x^{2}$$ . Then
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack x(2x^{2})\rbrack = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(2x^{3}) = 6x^{2}$$
On the other hand, $$f^{\prime}(x)g^{\prime}(x) = (1)(4x) = 4x$$ . So
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack \neq f^{\prime}(x)g^{\prime}(x)$$

section.heading: The Quotient Rule
section.paragraph: The derivative of the quotient of two differentiable functions is given by the following rule:
As an aid to remembering this expression, observe that it has the following form:

$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right\rbrack = \frac{({Denominator})\left( \begin{array}{l} {Derivative of} \\ {numerator} \end{array} \right) - ({Numerator})\left( \begin{array}{l} {Derivative of} \\ {denominator} \end{array} \right)}{({Square of denominator})}$$
For a proof of the Quotient Rule, see Exercise 74.
The derivative of a quotient is not equal to the quotient of the derivatives; that is,
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right\rbrack \neq \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$$
For example, if $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ , then
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right\rbrack = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{x^{3}}{x^{2}} \right) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x) = 1$$
which is not equal to
$$\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x^{3})}{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x^{2})} = \frac{3x^{2}}{2x} = \frac{3}{2}x$$

note.source_type: Applied Example 6. Rate of Change of DVD Sales
note.title: Applied Example 6. Rate of Change of DVD Sales
note.heading: Applied Example 6. Rate of Change of DVD Sales
note.paragraph: The annual sales (in millions of dollars per year) of a DVD recording of a hit movie $$t$$ years from the date of release is given by

list.item: Find the rate at which the annual sales are changing at time $$t$$ .
How fast are the annual sales changing at the time the DVDs are released $$(t = 0)$$ ? Two years from the date of release?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The rate at which the annual sales are changing at time $$t$$ is given by $$S^{\prime}(t)$$ . Using the Quotient Rule, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {S^{\prime}(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack \frac{5t}{t^{2} + 1} \right\rbrack = 5\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack \frac{t}{t^{2} + 1} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{S^{\prime}(t)} = 5\left\lbrack \frac{\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)(1) - t(2t)}{\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{S^{\prime}(t)} = 5\left\lbrack \frac{t^{2} + 1 - 2t^{2}}{\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack = \frac{5\left( 1 - t^{2} \right)}{\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$ Algebra See Example 2.

The rate at which the annual sales are changing at the time the DVDs are released is given by $$S^{\prime}(0) = \frac{5(1 - 0)}{(0 + 1)^{2}} = 5$$ That is, they are increasing at the rate of $$\$ 5$$ million per year per year. Two years from the date of release, the annual sales are changing at the rate of $$S^{\prime}(2) = \frac{5(1 - 4)}{(4 + 1)^{2}} = - \frac{3}{5} = - 0.6$$ That is, they are decreasing at the rate of $$\$ 600,000$$ per year per year. The graph of the function $$S$$ is shown in Figure 5. Figure 5 Details A graph plots a curve on a coordinate plane, where the horizontal axis t is marked from 0 to over 10 years and the vertical axis S(t) is marked from 0 to over 3 millions of dollars per year. The curve begins at the origin rises steeply to the right, bulging away from the x axis, veering only slightly from the vertical axis, reaches a peak at approximately (1, 2.5), from where it gradually descends bulging towards the x axis till around (10, 0.5). After a spectacular rise, the annual sales begin to taper off.

Use trace and zoom to determine the coordinates of the highest point on the graph of $$S$$ in the interval $$\lbrack 0,10\rbrack$$ . Interpret your results.

note.source_type: Applied Example 7. Oxygen-Restoration Rate in a Pond
note.title: Applied Example 7. Oxygen-Restoration Rate in a Pond
note.heading: Applied Example 7. Oxygen-Restoration Rate in a Pond
note.paragraph: When organic waste is dumped into a pond, the oxidation process that takes place reduces the pond’s oxygen content. However, given time, nature will restore the oxygen content to its natural level. Suppose the oxygen content $$t$$ days after organic waste has been dumped into the pond is given by

list.item: Derive a general expression that gives the rate of change of the pond’s oxygen level at any time $$t$$ .
How fast is the pond’s oxygen content changing $$1$$ day, $$10$$ days, and $$20$$ days after the organic waste has been dumped?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The rate of change of the pond’s oxygen level at any time $$t$$ is given by the derivative of the function $$f$$ . Thus, the required expression is $$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(t) = 100\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack \frac{t^{2} + 10t + 100}{t^{2} + 20t + 100} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{(t^{2} + 20t + 100)\frac{d}{dt}(t^{2} + 10t + 100) - (t^{2} + 10t + 100)\frac{d}{dt}(t^{2} + 20t + 100)}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)(2t + 10) - \left( t^{2} + 10t + 100 \right)(2t + 20)}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{2t^{3} + 10t^{2} + 40t^{2} + 200t + 200t + 1000 - 2t^{3} - 20t^{2} - 20t^{2} - 200t - 200t - 2000}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10t^{2} - 1000}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack \text{Combine like terms in the numerator.} } \end{array}$$ Algebra See Example 2.

The rate at which the pond’s oxygen content is changing $$1$$ day after the organic waste has been dumped is given by $$f^{\prime}(1) = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10 - 1000}{(1 + 20 + 100)^{2}} \right\rbrack \approx - 6.76$$ That is, it is dropping at the rate of $$6.8\%$$ per day. After $$10$$ days, the rate is $$f^{\prime}(10) = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10(10)^{2} - 1000}{{(10^{2} + 20(10) + 100)}^{2}} \right\rbrack = 0$$ That is, it is neither increasing nor decreasing. After $$20$$ days, the rate is $$f^{\prime}(20) = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10(20)^{2} - 1000}{{(20^{2} + 20(20) + 100)}^{2}} \right\rbrack \approx 0.37$$ That is, the oxygen content is increasing at the rate of $$0.37\%$$ per day, and the restoration process has indeed begun.

section.heading: Verification of the Product Rule
section.paragraph: We will now verify the Product Rule. If $$p(x) = f(x)g(x)$$ , then
$$p^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{p(x + h) - p(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h)g(x + h) - f(x)g(x)}{h}$$
By adding $$- f(x + h)g(x) + f(x + h)g(x)$$ (which is zero!) to the numerator and factoring, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {p^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h)\left\lbrack g(x + h) - g(x) \right\rbrack + g(x)\left\lbrack f(x + h) - f(x) \right\rbrack}{h}} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left\{ {f(x + h)\left\lbrack \frac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h} \right\rbrack + g(x)\left\lbrack \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} \right\rbrack} \right\}} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}f(x + h)\left\lbrack \frac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h} \right\rbrack + \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}g(x)\left\lbrack \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} \right\rbrack { \text{By Property} 3 \text{of limits} }} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}f(x + h) \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h} + \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}g(x) \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} { \text{By Property} 4 \text{of limits} }} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = f(x)g^{\prime}(x) + g(x)f^{\prime}(x)} \end{array}$$
Observe that in the last link in the chain of equalities, we have used the fact that $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}f(x + h) = f(x)$$ because $$f$$ is continuous at $$x$$ .

note.heading: Applied Example 2. Importance of Time in Treating Heart Attacks
note.paragraph: According to the American Heart Association, the treatment benefit for heart attacks depends on the time until treatment and is described by the function
where $$t$$ is measured in hours and $$f(t)$$ is expressed as a percent.

list.item: Use a graphing utility to graph the function $$f$$ using the viewing window $$\lbrack 0,24\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,100\rbrack$$ .
Use a graphing utility to find the derivative of $$f$$ when $$t = 0$$ and $$t = 2$$ .
Interpret the results obtained in part (b).

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The graph of $$f$$ is shown in Figure T2. Figure T2 Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane, where the horizontal axis is marked from 0 to 24 units and the vertical axis is marked from 0 to 100 units. The curve begins at the top at the 100 mark on the vertical axis at a high point, descends rightward, swelling slightly away from the y axis for a very short stretch and bulging downward toward the x axis in a long steep curve till approximately (6, 10), after which it continues to the right, running almost parallel and very close to the horizontal axis till it exits the viewing window in the bottom right corner.

Using the numerical derivative operation of a graphing utility, we find $$f^{\prime}(0) \approx 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(2) \approx - 28.95402429$$ (see Figure T3). Figure T3 Details The image shows two numerical derivative screens a and b. Numerical derivative screen a reads Line 1: n Deriv((.44x^4+700)/(.1x^4+7),x,0) Line 2: 0 Numerical derivative screen b reads Line 1: n Deriv((.44x^4+700)/(.1x^4+7),x,2) Line 2: negative 28.95402429 TI-83/84 numerical derivative screens (a) for computing $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ and (b) for computing $$f^{\prime}(2)$$

The results of part (b) show that there is no drop in the treatment benefit when the heart attack is treated immediately. But the treatment benefit drops off at the rate of approximately $$29\%$$ per hour when the time to treatment is $$2$$ hours. Thus, it is extremely urgent that a patient suffering a heart attack receive medical attention as soon as possible.
